                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                               REPLY COMMENTS OF VISTRA CORP.

            Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby respectfully submits these reply comments concerning the

     Secretary of Energy’s letter regarding the interconnection of large loads and the accompanying

     Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposal (“DOE ANOPR Proposal”) in the above-

     captioned proceeding.1

I.      Introduction

            While the extensive record of this proceeding reflects a wide range of views, there is

     general agreement on two fundamental issues. First, winning the AI race will require significant

     new digital infrastructure and energy infrastructure to generate and deliver power.2 Second, that

     infrastructure must be developed in the most efficient way possible.3

            The need for reform is clear and urgent. Regulatory uncertainty is stymying data center

     development and the Commission’s inaction in its most significant proceedings involving data

quo is insufficient to build the infrastructure necessary to meet the moment.5 That is simply not

an acceptable outcome.

       To win the AI race, the United States needs to maximize the use of the infrastructure that

we already have, in the short term, while building out a more robust electric grid in the medium-

to-long term. To maximize use of existing infrastructure, the Commission must prioritize the

issues on which it can make the most immediate and meaningful progress. Accordingly, Vistra

reiterates that the Commission should pursue the following path:

          First, the Commission should issue—as soon as possible—unequivocal determinations
           (either in Docket No. EL25-49 et al., other pending docket(s), or in this docket) that
           provide immediate clarity on how existing rules should be applied while the
           Commission works to implement reforms in this proceeding. Doing so will help ensure
           that this important proceeding does not become a roadblock to concluding the
           commercial arrangements needed to unlock investment. In particular, the Commission
           should make clear:

                  The co-location of large loads with existing generation resources is permissible
                   under existing rules, including generator modification rules,6 and the
                   “necessary study” process.7
                  Cost causation principles require that the parties to such an arrangement fund
                   any necessary network upgrades, and the transmission service that facilitates

                     developed in this proceeding to co-location with existing generation.10

                   Third, the Commission should exercise its jurisdiction to establish new transmission-
                   level load interconnection procedures for loads that are not co-located with generation
                   resources—i.e., loads that do not share a point of interconnection with a generator.
                   Standalone load interconnections are no less important than other load
                   interconnections, but the associated rules may be more time consuming to develop.
                   The Commission could propose those reforms in this rulemaking docket or establish a
                   separate docket for that purpose, but in any event those reforms should not hold up the
                   above reforms related to co-location. As described below, this step is fully consistent
                   with the Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission. This represents a new
                   application of the Commission’s jurisdiction and the area where it has the least
                   familiarity and experience. As such, Vistra believes it would behoove the Commission
                   to take a more measured approach here and develop the record necessary to ensure that
                   its reforms fully realize the goals and transformative potential of Secretary Wright’s
                   proposal.

               The balance of these comments provides more detail on how the Commission should move

      forward on co-location (including co-location involving existing generation and co-location

      involving new generation) and standalone transmission-level load interconnection.

II.      Co-Location

               A wide range of commenters across all segments of the industry agree that the co-location

      of loads and generation is one of the most promising vehicles to get the most out of existing

      infrastructure.11 Regardless of the configuration, co-location can minimize the system impacts of

      new large loads and reduce the need for costly network upgrades.12 In the short term, co-location

      therefore represents one of the best ways to build the digital infrastructure needed to win the AI

      race. As discussed below, while all types of co-location should be facilitated and incentivized, the




      —————————————————
         11

 procedures by which the Commission can do so will vary depending on whether the co-location

arrangement involves an existing generator or a new generator.

         A. Types of Co-location

                  1. Co-location with Existing Generation

         Co-location of new loads with existing generation resources is the lowest hanging fruit for

Commission action because both the infrastructure and the rules to facilitate the use thereof already

exist. Further, there is a fully briefed Commission docket, with an extensive record, in which the

Commission can act to facilitate these arrangements. As Vistra has previously explained, the

Commission should issue unequivocal determinations in Docket No. EL25-49 et al, and/or other

pending docket(s), to provide immediate clarity on how existing rules should be applied. While

the Commission could consider changing those rules in the context of future reforms in this

proceeding, as discussed below, the Commission must not allow parties that seek to delay new

large load interconnections to use this important proceeding to freeze the industry and prevent the

rapid development of digital infrastructure needed to win the AI race.

         The record in this proceeding provides further support for these arrangements. As multiple

commenters explain, the technologies required to facilitate the co-location of new loads behind-

the-meter at existing generating facilities are reliable and technically sound. For instance, CAISO

explains that “strict, unwavering protections like circuit breakers at their point of interconnection”

can maintain reliability with “only those network upgrades necessary based on the requested net

[withdrawal and injection] rights.”13       ENGIE explains that the “[t]echnology to prevent




—————————————————

 unauthorized flows exists and is currently in use.”14 ODEC similarly notes that its distribution

cooperative members are already installing similar system protection devices on storage

facilities.15

          While some commenters appear to limit their support of co-location arrangements only to

co-located facilities involving new generation,16 such an approach will produce counterproductive

results because retaining existing generation is critical to resource adequacy.17 The record also

supports the proposition that the Commission need not create a new resource adequacy study to

facilitate co-location of new loads with existing generators. As PSEG explains, such studies are

not performed even for retiring generators, and adding an evaluation of resource adequacy issues

for co-located load arrangements would be “unnecessary, inefficient, unduly discriminatory, and

not the correct legal or practical fit for these arrangements.”18 It would be remarkably inefficient—

and unduly discriminatory—to inadvertently incentivize the retirement of existing generation at

exactly the wrong moment by creating barriers to the co-location of new loads with existing

generating facilities.

                    2. Co-location with New Generation

          After the Commission clarifies how existing rules should be applied to co-location

arrangements involving existing generation, the Commission should prioritize reforms to facilitate

the interconnection of co-location arrangements involving new load and new generation. The

development of these facilities without protracted litigation. Even commenters that contest the

 Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission-level load interconnection acknowledge that the

Commission has clear jurisdiction over the interconnection of co-located facilities.25 The reason

is simple: the Commission has long exercised jurisdiction over generator interconnection, and

“the Commission does not lose its jurisdiction over the interconnection simply because a load also

happens to interconnect to the interstate grid at the same point.”26

         In short, there is no reasonable jurisdictional basis to contest the Commission’s ability to

regulate the interconnection of co-located facilities. Therefore, the Commission can proceed with

implementing reforms to facilitate the interconnection of co-located facilities more quickly, while

it resolves the more complex issues raised in the ANOPR on a slightly longer timeline.

         Constellation raises the valid concern that a process to expedite the coordinated study of

co-location arrangements involving new generation would be unduly discriminatory against

existing generation because it would incentivize load to co-locate only with new generation.27 But

the Commission can design a process that alleviates those concerns.           As noted above, the

Commission should clarify that existing generator modification rules, including the necessary

study process, can be used to add co-located load to an existing generator’s point of

interconnection. In the context of that clarification, the Commission could indicate that it intends

to keep those rules in place moving forward and that those rules must provide load interconnection

on a timeline no longer than the equivalent process to facilitate load co-location with new

generation. Alternatively, the Commission could clarify that those rules will continue to apply

eventually replace those existing rules and apply equally to co-location arrangements with new

and existing generation resources.28 Either approach can avoid undue discrimination provided it

accommodates co-location configurations in a comparable manner and on a comparable timeline

regardless of whether they involve new or existing generation. And either approach would be

workable as long as it applies only prospectively and does not disrupt existing commercial

agreements or projects already being studied.

          While some commenters suggest that the Commission divert its resources to address

resource adequacy issues through other mechanisms outside the scope of this proceeding, like

nationalizing PJM’s reliability backstop auction,29 Vistra believes that the Commission can

address those issues by unlocking the potential of co-location. Many large load developers seek

to pair their loads with generation, but the lack of clear and coordinated processes to effectuate

those configurations has stymied that development.30 Facilitating and incentivizing these facilities

will unleash a flood of private capital to help bolster resource adequacy across the country while

focusing cost recovery for new generation on the entities that desire it.

          B. Substantive Principles for Co-Location

          Certain substantive principles should apply equally to all types of co-location

configurations. The DOE ANOPR Proposal correctly provides that transmission providers should

          A host of commenters agree that identifying a co-located facility’s network upgrades and

charging it for transmission service based on its actual use of the transmission system ensures the

reliable interconnection of co-located facilities without overestimating their impact on the

transmission system, maximizing the efficiency of transmission system buildout, to the benefit of

load customers and other retail ratepayers.36 Doing so also comports with cost causation, ensuring

that load customers—particularly load customers fully funding upgrades under a participant

funding arrangement—are not obliged to pay the full costs of upgrades for which they are not the

“but for” cause, and are not forced to take or pay for transmission service that they do not actually

use.37 Finally, providing transmission service to co-located facilities based on their actual use of

the transmission system will incentivize more new large loads to interconnect via co-location,

which is undoubtedly the large load interconnection model most likely to fulfill speed-to-power

needs while minimizing strain on the grid.38

necessary to reliably enable this approach. For example, CAISO explains that the Commission

well as other measures necessary to ensure reliable operation of the transmission system.

Importantly, the Commission must ensure that any such requirements are just and reasonable and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

customer’s actual usage of the transmission system are unpersuasive.43 The record in this

proceeding indicates that transmission providers can—and already do—rely on system protection

III.      There Are Multiple Policy Options for Allocating Network Upgrade Costs

               There is much debate in the record over who should pay for the network upgrades needed

       to interconnect new large loads, regardless of whether they are co-located with generation. While

       a number of commenters support the ANOPR’s principle that new loads should be responsible for

       100% of the network upgrade costs they require,48 many transmission providers oppose that

       principle and suggest that they should roll the costs of those network upgrades into rate base.49

               Notwithstanding that debate, commenters recognize that the Commission cannot depart

       from its prohibition on “and” pricing.50 Any network upgrade cost allocation method must adhere

       to the longstanding rule that a transmission provider may charge a transmission customer either

       the incremental cost of expanding the transmission system to provide the customer’s requested

       service, or the embedded costs of the transmission system with expansion costs rolled in, but not

    1. Participant Funding:53 The large load customer pays the incremental cost of upgrades

IV.      Standalone Load Interconnection

               After the Commission addresses the issues that are most readily solvable in the near-term,

      it should proceed to exercise jurisdiction to regulate load interconnection to the transmission

      system for loads that are not co-located with generation resources. These reforms may be more

      time consuming to develop because they represent a new application of the Commission’s

      jurisdiction. However, as indicated below, Vistra believes that this step is fully consistent with the

      Commission’s jurisdiction, there is a clear need for reform to prevent undue discrimination, and a

      more standardized load interconnection process could bring a host of other benefits.

               A. Jurisdiction

      the transmission system, none do so in a thorough or persuasive manner. For instance, several

      commenters rely on arguments that the DOE ANOPR Proposal will infringe on state authority

      over siting or the terms of retail sales.65 But as Vistra explained at length in its initial comments,

      it is entirely possible for FERC to regulate the interconnection process without infringing on these

      state jurisdictional issues. Indeed, Vistra’s Exhibit A illustrates the extent to which federal

      jurisdiction over load interconnection to the transmission system would not impact existing state

V.      Conclusion

              The Commission now has an extensive record on which to act to ensure the “timely,

     orderly, and non-discriminatory” interconnection of large loads to the transmission system. Vistra

     submits that the Commission should prioritize the issues on which it can make the most immediate

     and meaningful progress. Specifically, Vistra believes that the Commission can make the most

     significant progress in the near term by facilitating co-location with existing generators under

     currently effective filed rates and then focusing on reforms related to the co-location of large load

     and new generation. Doing so will position the industry to meet new demand while maximizing

     the use of existing infrastructure and minimizing strain on the grid.
